header: Date: 2026-03-26; Time: 15:00-15:52 UTC; Duration: 52 minutes; Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Karen O'Neill (CISO - Harris Trust), Mark Reynolds (Head Cloud Architecture), Sanjay Rao (Legal), Priya Shah (Platform Eng), Tom Briggs (VP Digital)
summary: Discovery focused on data residency, logging restrictions, and compliance requirements for potential Redwood deployment. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for financial services controls; primary constraints include US-only data residency, SOC2/HIPAA considerations for specific products, strict logging/PII retention policies, and SSO/KMS requirements. Agreed next step is security deep-dive and delivery of compliance artifacts.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Network architecture / VPC peering / on-prem options
transcript:
[00:00] Laura Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Laura, account exec at Redwood. With me is Diego, our SE. Could we quick intros?
[00:08] Karen O'Neill: Karen, CISO at Harris Trust. We lead security and compliance for digital channels.
[00:12] Mark Reynolds: Mark, cloud architecture. We run most of our workloads in us-east-1 and an on-prem VPC in Chicago.
[00:16] Sanjay Rao: Sanjay, legal counsel. We'll be focusing on contractual controls around data residency and logging.
[00:21] Diego Martinez: Hey all, Diego, solutions engineer. I'll jump into architecture stuff.
[00:25] Laura: Thanks. High level, we want to understand your must-have constraints for running Redwood — hosted API, dedicated, or private. Karen, can you kick off with requirements?
[00:34] Karen: Sure. First, data residency — any customer data used for inference must stay within US jurisdictions. No EU or other regions for now. Second, auditability — we need immutable audit logs with 7 year retention for certain financial products. Third, logging restrictions: transcripts that contain PII need to be redacted or not stored. And finally, encryption at rest and in transit - KMS is a hard req, HSM preferred for key management.
[00:57] Laura: Got it. Diego, quick comment on how Redwood handles those?
[01:01] Diego: Absolutely. For Hosted we offer region-specific hosting (we can pin to us-east-1 or a US-only region), but note that for some customers the Hosted control plane is multi-tenant and logs metadata. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and stronger isolation — logs still flow through Redwood's control plane unless configured differently. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives the most control: CCTV private — sorry, I mean private control plane with customer-managed network and optional on-prem package. With Private we can also integrate customer KMS/HSM so keys never leave your environment.
[01:33] Mark: When you say Hosted can be pinned, does that mean the inference data stays in the US? Or are there backups that might cross regions?
[01:39] Diego: Yes, inference compute and storage can be pinned to US-only. For backups and long-term storage we have policies; by default we keep backups in the same region, but we need to make that explicit in the contract — we can put it in the SOC2 addendum. Some of the backup tooling is eventual consistency and could land in other US regions if you allow. We can restrict to specific AZs/regions in Dedicated/Private modes.
[02:05] Karen: We also have a concern about logging: our legal team will not accept raw transcript storage in a third-party multi-tenant hosted environment for certain regulated workflows. What are options to turn off transcript retention or to redact PII automatically?
[02:16] Diego: Good question. We have a few levers: 1) Disable transcript retention at the tenant level for Hosted — that means we don't persist the full text, only minimal usage metrics. 2) Use automatic pii redaction pipelines before storage — but that adds latency and is config dependent. 3) For full control, Private deployment lets you host logs in your VPC or on-prem object store, so Redwood doesn't retain raw transcripts. There's also a 'no-logging' mode for sensitive endpoints where only token counts are logged.
[02:44] Sanjay: If you say 'no-logging' mode, do you still collect metadata that could be considered personal data? For compliance we need clarity on what metadata is collected and where it's stored.
[02:52] Diego: We collect minimal metadata: timestamp, model variant, token counts, and request IDs. We can provide a ledger of what fields are captured. In Private/Dedicated we can disable even some of those fields from leaving the VPC.
[03:04] Priya Shah: Network-wise, for Private deployment do you support VPC peering and cross-account roles? Our infra team needs to control egress via our NAT and have no direct inbound from the internet.
[03:12] Diego: Yes — Private offers VPC peering, transit gateway attachments, or on-prem connectors. We can run the control plane either in your VPC or in a customer-managed VPC with a private endpoint. For Dedicated we usually do secure VPN and peering to Redwood-managed VPCs; egress rules can be restrictive.
[03:29] Tom Briggs: What about SSO and RBAC? We need SAML 2.0 and SCIM provisioning and roles mapped to our corporate groups.
[03:35] Laura: We support SSO SAML and SCIM — you can map groups to Redwood roles and restrict access to production models. We'll include our SAML docs in the follow-up.
[03:41] Karen: Encryption — you mentioned KMS/HSM. For Private, can we bring our own HSM and have keys never leave our environment?
[03:47] Diego: Yes. Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations (both cloud KMS and network HSM attachments). For Dedicated we can support cross-account KMS where the key policy restricts Redwood's role but keys live in your cloud account. For Hosted you'd use Redwood-managed KMS unless you sign an enterprise contract that allows customer KMS in a dedicated tenancy.
[04:08] Mark: Latency tradeoffs — Private sounded great for compliance, but will we pay a latency tax? We have low-latency SLAs for some services.
[04:15] Diego: Private on-prem will be lowest latency if it's colocated near your services. Hosted can be low-latency if our region matches yours, Dedicated provides predictable throughput. The biggest latency hit is when you add heavy redaction or external KMS operations for each request — that can add tens to hundreds of milliseconds depending on key design. We can cache K V — KV cache — to reduce repeated KMS ops for session keys.
[04:38] Mark: Are there options to use local encryption keys but have tokenization performed by Redwood? We're trying to avoid exporting PII.
[04:44] Diego: You can tokenize or pseudonymize client-side before sending. Alternatively, a Private deployment where the tokenization service runs in your VPC is common. We also support transformers that perform in-flight redaction using a small model to strip PII before logging, but that requires validation.
[05:03] Karen: On contracts: do you have specific clauses for financial regulators on audit support? For example, we may need evidence of who accessed what model and when — ordered by user.
[05:12] Laura: We provide audit logs with user IDs, model version, request IDs and timestamps. For Dedicated and Private we can extend retention and provide exportable logs for audits. We'll attach an example audit log schema.
[05:22] Sanjay: We will need an SLA about data deletion too — if a customer requests deletion, how quickly can you purge backups and cached KV?
[05:29] Diego: Deletion in Hosted is subject to backup cycles; we can offer contractual deletion windows (e.g., 30 days) and for Dedicated/Private we can guarantee immediate deletion if keys are rotated and data is inaccessible. For stronger guarantees, Private with customer-managed storage is best.
[05:44] Mark: Cost questions — how does Dedicated pricing compare to Hosted if we need high throughput and US-only regions?
[05:50] Laura: Dedicated is a committed capacity model, so unit cost per token is lower but requires an upfront reserved capacity. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. We'll include pricing examples in the follow-up.
[05:58] Priya: For POC, we want to run a pilot on a subset of traffic (non-customer-facing) to validate redaction, latency, and integration. Will Redwood support a short pilot in Private/Dedicated?
[06:07] Diego: Yes — we usually do a 4-6 week pilot; we can spin up a small Dedicated pool or a Private sandbox depending on the controls you need. For immediate testing we can provide a Hosted sandbox with logging disabled to validate integration, but for compliance testing Private is better.
[06:22] Laura: Let's walk through a hypothetical secure flow — Priya, what's your preferred architecture?
[06:26] Priya: Ideally, requests originate from our app servers in us-east-1, pass through a tokenization proxy that strips PII, then talk to the inference tier. We want SAML enforced for access and logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[06:35] Diego: That maps well. In Private we can place the tokenization proxy in your VPC, have a private endpoint to the inference cluster, integrate KMS for key ops, and forward logs to your SIEM via syslog or an event bridge.
[06:45] Mark: What about model updates? We need stable model versioning and controlled rollouts.
[06:49] Laura: Redwood supports pinned model versions, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback policies. For Dedicated and Private you'll control which artifacts are promoted to prod.
[06:57] Tom: Audit demands sometimes want verbatim transcripts for legal review. But earlier you said we might need to not store transcripts — is there an approach to satisfy both?
[07:05] Diego: We can implement dual paths: store verbatim transcripts in your on-prem archive accessible only to legal, while Redwood retains zero or redacted copies. That requires Private and explicit contract language about storage location and access controls.
[07:18] Sanjay: Also need to confirm export controls and data subject access requests. We need mechanisms to locate and remove a subject's data across logs and backups.
[07:25] Diego: We'll provide our data subject request playbook; with Private deployments it's simpler since you control storage. For Hosted we'll need to map where artifacts are stored to ensure removals cascade — we can add that to the compliance addendum.
[07:38] Karen: A couple of nitty-gritty questions: 1) Can you disable telemetry like model telemetry? 2) How do you handle debug logs which often contain payloads?
[07:45] Diego: Telemetry toggles exist — in Dedicated and Private you can disable or limit telemetry. Debug logs are opt-in and we recommend never enabling them in prod for PII-bearing endpoints.
[07:55] Laura: Quick pause — any other major blockers?
[07:58] Mark: Data residency and logging are blockers but not deal stoppers. We need to see docs and an architecture we can sign off on.
[08:03] Karen: Also contractual language around breach notifications and subprocessor lists — can we get that?
[08:07] Laura: Yes, we'll include subprocessor list and breach notification timelines.
[08:10] Diego: I'll flag the network and KMS items for a follow-up with your infra team.
[08:15] Priya: If we do Private, how long to spin up an environment for a pilot?
[08:19] Diego: Typically 2-4 weeks for a Private sandbox with our standard automation; Dedicated can be faster if you accept Redwood-managed infra.
[08:27] Sanjay: On legal timeline, we typically need 6-8 weeks for vendor review after we receive security artifacts. So earlier the better.
[08:33] Laura: Noted. We'll prioritize SOC2 and architecture docs.
[08:36] Diego: Quick technical note — about the KV cache and redaction: caching reduces KMS calls but be mindful of storing any sensitive tokens in the cache unless you use transient keys. We can show example cache lifetimes and encryption at rest for those caches.
[08:51] Mark: If we use caching, who controls key rotation?
[08:54] Diego: In Private, you control rotation via your KMS. In Dedicated we can coordinate cross-account rotation. Hosted uses Redwood-managed rotation unless contracted otherwise.
[09:03] Laura: We're getting low on time. I'll recap.
[09:06] Laura: Action items: Laura sends SOC2 & SAML docs; Diego sends Private deployment diagram and KMS/HSM notes; Harris provides region list and data classification. We'll schedule a security deep-dive next week. Any objections?
[09:18] Karen: No objections. That's fine.
[09:21] Tom: Sounds good. We also want a pricing sketch for Dedicated vs Private pilot.
[09:25] Laura: We'll include that. Anything else?
[09:28] Priya: Please include sample log schema and retention options.
[09:31] Diego: Will do.
[09:34] Laura: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the deep-dive.
[09:40] Sanjay: Thanks.
[09:41] Mark: Thank you.
[09:42] (call ends)
